subject: Business
title: The Pareto Principle in Business
description: A 60-second lesson on The Pareto Principle in Business.

hook.text: 80% of your revenue comes from 20% of your customers. Vilfredo Pareto noticed this pattern everywhere.

buildup.text: The 80/20 rule says a small number of inputs produce the majority of outputs in most systems.

discovery.text: 20% of bugs cause 80% of crashes. 20% of products generate 80% of sales. The pattern is remarkably consistent.

twist.text: Most companies spread resources evenly. The winners focus disproportionately on the vital few.

climax.text: Apple has a tiny product line compared to Samsung. Fewer products, more focus, higher margins.

punchline.text: Find the 20% that matters. Ignore the rest.

quiz.question: What does the Pareto Principle suggest?
options: A small percentage of inputs produces the majority of outputs
Focus should always be on cost reduction

details.summary: The Pareto Principle observes that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes. In business, 80% of profits typically come from 20% of customers, 80% of complaints from 20% of products, and 80% of sales from 20% of the sales team.
details.whyItMatters: The Pareto Principle helps prioritize limited resources for maximum impact. Identifying the vital few customers, products, or activities that drive most results enables focused investment rather than spreading resources thinly across all areas.
takeaways: A small percentage of inputs typically drives a large percentage of outcomes
Identifying the vital few focuses resources where they create most value
The principle applies across sales, complaints, defects, and most business metrics

faq.question: Is the 80/20 split always exactly accurate?
faq.answer: No. The actual distribution varies and might be 70/30 or 90/10. The principle is directional: a minority of inputs drives a majority of outputs. The exact ratio matters less than the insight that impact is distributed very unevenly and focused effort yields disproportionate results.

faq.question: How should businesses apply the Pareto Principle practically?
faq.answer: Identify your highest-value customers and prioritize their retention. Focus quality improvement on the few product defects causing most complaints. Allocate sales resources to the highest-potential accounts. Cut or reduce investment in the many activities generating minimal returns.
